Preisser prosented a draft proposal that would create a special committee of ‘College Liaisons.’ He briefly outlined the need for such a special committee and provided some background on how the idea emerged from the Executive Committee more than two years ago and how it has evolved since then.
The Committee members would have two main responsibilities, with that scope of work having been refined with the input of the college deans.

On behalf of the faculty of the College of Education, we would like to revisit a concern previously expressed by our college regarding this fall’s academic calendar, as it relates to classes being held on Columbus Day/ Indigenous Peoples’ Day while offices were closed.
We believe the relevance of this issue extends beyond any single college and has implications for the university as a whole.
We recognize the challenge faced by the faculty senate’s calendar committee when planning for semesters that must be compressed due to the need for the university to start classes after Labor Day, and would like to suggest a University Manual (UM) change to simplify this process in the future.
We also recognize and are proud that URI has made a clear commitment to acknowledging and honoring the Narragansett Nation and Niantic People on whose land we reside.
Holding classes on Columbus Day/ Indigenous Peoples’ Day, particularly when the institution is otherwise formally observing the day through office closures, creates a misalignment between our stated values and our academic practices.

This tension has the potential to be felt most strongly by our Native students, faculty, staff, and community partners.
Although our primary focus in revising guidance provided by the UM for future calendars is related to aligning the process with our institution’s values, we also believe there are additional concerns to consider in holding classes on days when students and faculty do not have access to critical offices across campus.
For example, students requiring accommodations may be denied them due to the Testing Center and Disability Access and Inclusion Office being closed.
In addition, as was experienced on Monday October 12, 2026, offices being closed results in faculty not having access to staff who are critical to their ability to deliver the curriculum and to ensure the safety of students.
We recognize the need to preserve the required number of instructional days in years when the academic calendar is compressed.
Our proposal does not reduce instructional time; rather, it changes which traditional non-instructional day is converted to an instructional day.

Given the significance of this issue to our institutional mission and public commitments, we are asking that the FSEC assist us in refining the guidance for designing the academic calendar in these circumstances provided by the UM so that it reflects our commitment to our indigenous neighbors.
This can be accomplished by changing how the traditional fall non-instructional days are re-prioritized so that Columbus Day/Indigenous Peoples’ Day is recognized as a non-instructional day before the Wednesday before Thanksgiving.
We would like the Faculty Senate to consider a language change in the UM to provide guidelines for future calendars: In cases where the fall semester starts late enough to require one of our traditional no-class days to be sacrificed, we would turn the Wednesday before Thanksgiving into a class day.

2025-26 Academic Year Annual Report of the Joint Committee for Academic Program Review & Outcomes Assessment to the Faculty Senate The following report is an update on student learning outcomes assessment for the 2025-2026 academic assessment reporting year and reaffirms that student learning outcomes and academic program review is acknowledged as a shared responsibility and demonstrates a regular and ongoing commitment to understanding student learning and student success.
Data and results from outcomes assessment activities are examined in the aggregate only and are not used to evaluate individual faculty nor students, but to improve learning opportunities for all students.
SUMMARY OF INSTITUTION WIDE ASSESSMENT ACTIVITIES The summary of outcomes assessment reporting presents the assessment activities of the Joint Committee for Student Learning Outcomes Assessment & Accreditation (JAPROA) that took place during the 2025-26 academic year.

Often throughout the year, and in support of this committee and its charge, members of the Office for the Advancement of Teaching & Learning (ATL), through the Office of Student Learning Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation (SLOAA), acted in partnership to ensure specific objectives were met and certain expertise related goals were achieved.
The following items describe the work accomplished by this committee.
Item #1: New Program Assessment Plans During the 2025-26 academic year, the JAPROA continued to partner with members of ATL through SLOAA to ensure that new assessment plan proposals received timely support and guidance as part of new degree program and certificate offerings.
This process has ensured compliance with the Faculty Senate’s current program proposal process. (ref: University Manual 8.85.14 .).
The review of assessment plans includes the articulation of program goals, learning outcomes, curriculum map support, and a plan for long-term learning for each program.
This year, 9 degree program assessment plans were reviewed and supported, and 12 certificate assessment plans were reviewed and supported.

Please see Appendix A for a complete list of those specific degree and certificate programs.
Item #2: New Program Process Workflow Part of the charge given to JAPROA from the Faculty Senate’s Executive Committee this year was to support and provide additional clarification about the process that new programs (degrees and certificates) must follow in order to attain Faculty Senate support from their originating department.
Members of this committee took on that charge and the following workflow visual was developed.
Please see Appendix B to review the resource.
Item #3: Student Learning Outcomes Assessment Process Review and Update For years, the Student Learning Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation team in the Office for the Advancement of Teaching & Learning has provided support to all URI colleges and departments as it relates to the effective evaluation of student learning outcomes in the undergraduate curriculum.
Historically, the evaluation of student learning outcomes at URI happened on a 2-year cycle, until the fall of 2024 when the university’s largest college, the College of Arts & Sciences, was collaboratively shifted by request to a 3-year cycle.

Since then, members of SLOAA have listened to other university leaders (Deans, Associate Deans, and Department Chairs, and individual faculty) from colleges across URI regarding this topic.
During the fall 2025 semester, members of ATL reached out to more than 50 other universities to learn more about their assessment processes.
From those conversations, along with receiving support from the Office of the Provost, we worked during the 2025-2026 academic year to reset the university’s undergraduate academic program assessment cycle to a 3-year schedule.
To learn more about this process, visit the Undergraduate Academic Program Assessment cycle webpage available through SLOAA.
Item #4: Undergraduate Academic Program Assessment Cycle Continuation Academic programs at the University of Rhode Island (URI) progress through distinct phases within an established assessment cycle.
This cycle was temporarily suspended during the 2025–2026 academic year. 1

Following her appointment in March 2026, Kim Richard, Associate Director of Student Learning Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation (SLOAA), and Chris Lavan, Associate Vice Provost for the Advancement of Teaching and Learning, met with academic deans and associate deans across all colleges to introduce the revised assessment cycle and reporting protocol.
Several department chairs subsequently requested reporting extensions based on the following institutional factors: ● Baseline Plan Development: Certain programs lacked prior engagement in the formal assessment process, necessitating the initial design of curriculum maps and assessment frameworks. ● Leadership Transition and Onboarding: Newly appointed department chairs required consultation regarding SLOAA protocols. ● Accreditation Alignment: Multiple units—specifically within engineering, business, and education—requested schedule adjustments to synchronize URI assessment deadlines with external specialized accreditation cycles.
Appendix C delineates the required submission deadlines for assessment reports to SLOAA, categorized by college and program.

Item #5: Revising and Editing the Assessment Form Also, during the 2025-26 academic year, new Associate Director for Student Learning Outcomes Assessment & Accreditation, Kim Richard, who brings 30 years of expertise from successful work led at multiple colleges and universities in the areas of teaching and learning, assessment of student learning, and NECHE accreditation, began to work towards modernizing and improving the assessment processes led by SLOAA to ensure alignment between JAPROA’s charge and NECHE accreditation expectations.
An example of this work is through the Undergraduate Academic Program Assessment Process and the subsequent form used to attain the information necessary to complete institutional accreditation requirements.
Discussions with multiple college leaders (Deans, Assistant and Associate Deans, as well as college-level assessment committees) to obtain their feedback on the previous process were held and updates were made accordingly.
The work is continuing with a goal of completion set for the fall 2026 semester in time for the aforementioned “restart” of the undergraduate academic assessment process.
